topics.name: Managers and management
topics.why: Definitions, levels, skills and roles. Learn the lists, then practise applying them to a real manager.
topics.notes:
Written from standard management theory. Your Week 1–2 slides are PDFs, so check these terms against them.

Management is getting things done efficiently and effectively through and with other people.

  • Efficiency = doing things right: getting the most output from the least input (resources).
  • Effectiveness = doing the right things: achieving the organisation's goals.
LevelWhoFocus
TopCEO, MD, directorsStrategy, long-term direction
MiddleDepartment and regional managersTurning strategy into plans, managing managers
First-lineSupervisors, team leadersDay-to-day operations, front-line staff

Katz's three skills: technical (most needed at first-line level), human (needed at every level), conceptual (most needed at top level).

Functions (from Fayol): Planning, Organising, Leading (commanding/directing), Coordinating, Controlling.

Mintzberg's 10 roles (from watching what managers actually do: brief, fragmented, varied work, not neat planning):

GroupRoles
InterpersonalFigurehead, Leader, Liaison
InformationalMonitor, Disseminator, Spokesperson
DecisionalEntrepreneur, Disturbance handler, Resource allocator, Negotiator

Apply it to a real manager, e.g. Elliott Hill (Nike CEO, from intern to CEO): figurehead at launches, spokesperson to investors, entrepreneur in strategy shifts, disturbance handler when sales fall.

topics.name: Classical theory: Taylor, Fayol, Weber
topics.why: The sample exam question is on this. Practise the 'why then?' and 'which organisations benefit?' answers.
topics.notes:
Why early theory emerged when it did: the Industrial Revolution brought rapid industrialisation, large factories, mass standardised production and a big unskilled workforce. Work was inconsistent and rule-of-thumb, with no formal way to organise, supervise and control it. Managers needed efficiency and consistency.

Taylor: scientific management asked "how do we do each task most efficiently?" Time-and-motion study to find the one best way, standardised tools and methods, scientific selection and training of workers, piece-rate pay, and a split between managers (plan) and workers (do). Standardisation fixed inconsistency, so products got better.

Fayol: administrative theory asked "how do we organise the whole organisation?" He was an engineer who rose to MD of a French mining company and turned it from near-insolvency to excellent condition. His managerial functions are planning, organising, commanding, coordinating and controlling. Of the 14 principles, the top 6 are division of work, unity of command, scalar chain, unity of direction, authority and responsibility, and equity. The rest: discipline, subordination of individual interest, remuneration, centralisation, order, stability of tenure, initiative, esprit de corps.

Weber: bureaucracy. Clear hierarchy of authority, division of labour, written rules and procedures, impersonality, selection and promotion on merit and qualifications, careers, and records.

Taylor vs Fayol at TUS: Taylor would time how fast staff process a registration. Fayol would ask how admissions are planned, how departments are organised, and whether there's a clear line of command.

Who benefits (exam favourite): organisations that need consistency and efficiency, such as hotel chains, Revenue, telecom call centres, Ryanair, banks and Revolut. Who doesn't: creative organisations like Electric Picnic, the Rose of Tralee or gaming studios, where rigid rules restrict flexibility and innovation and put creative people off.

Criticisms: treats workers like machines, ignores social and psychological needs, which led to the behavioural school (Mayo).

topics.name: Motivation: Maslow, Mayo, Herzberg
topics.why: Three theories, each with findings to apply. Flashcards first, then exam answers.
topics.notes:
Maslow's hierarchy (bottom up): physiological (pay for food and shelter) → safety (job security, safe conditions, pension) → social (teams, belonging) → esteem (recognition, status, promotion) → self-actualisation (challenge, growth). A satisfied need no longer motivates, so managers must find the employee's current level.

Mayo: the Hawthorne Studies (Western Electric, Chicago, 1924–33) began the behavioural (human relations) school, 1920–45.

  • Productivity rose whatever the lighting change. Workers responded to the attention: the Hawthorne effect.
  • Informal groups exert strong social control over work habits. Workers act as a group, not as individuals.
  • Recognition, security and belonging matter more to morale than physical conditions.
  • Money isn't the only motivator. Supervisors have significant influence on output.
  • Group collaboration must be planned and developed.

Herzberg's two-factor theory (motivation-hygiene), influenced by Maslow. Interviews with workers, engineers and accountants found satisfaction and dissatisfaction aren't on one scale.

Hygiene factors (extrinsic)Motivators (intrinsic)
Pay, job security, working conditions, company policy, supervision, relationships with colleaguesAchievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement, growth
Absent → dissatisfaction. Present → no dissatisfaction, but NOT motivationPresent → real motivation and satisfaction

Fixing a hygiene problem (low pay, bad supervision) removes complaints but rarely creates drive. Hygiene factors have a ceiling. This is why some HR programmes don't work.

topics.name: Business environment
topics.why: PESTEL, SWOT and five forces are frameworks you apply to a case. Practise writing, not just listing.
topics.notes:
Written from standard management theory. Your Week 1–2 slides are PDFs, so check these terms against them.

PESTEL scans the external macro-environment: Political (government stability, trade policy, Brexit), Economic (interest rates, inflation, unemployment, exchange rates), Social (demographics, lifestyle trends), Technological (AI, automation, e-commerce), Environmental (climate, carbon tax, sustainability), Legal (employment law, GDPR, consumer law).

Globalisation is the growing integration of economies through trade, investment, technology and the movement of people. Drivers: technology, falling transport costs, trade agreements (EU single market), multinationals. Opportunities: bigger markets, cheaper inputs, economies of scale. Threats: global competition, supply-chain risk, exposure to shocks elsewhere. Ireland is a small open economy that depends heavily on FDI.

SWOT: Strengths and Weaknesses are internal. Opportunities and Threats are external (they often come from the PESTEL). Match strengths to opportunities, and fix the weaknesses that expose you to threats.

Porter's five forces (industry competitiveness): threat of new entrants, bargaining power of suppliers, bargaining power of buyers, threat of substitutes, and rivalry among existing competitors. Strong forces mean lower industry profitability.

Exam tip: apply every factor to the case company (Purcells in the case study). Generic lists score poorly.

written.q: Using Mintzberg's managerial roles, analyse the work of a manager you know or have researched (e.g. Elliott Hill, CEO of Nike). Distinguish efficiency from effectiveness in your answer.
points: Mintzberg observed what managers actually do: brief, varied, fragmented work
Interpersonal roles with examples: figurehead, leader, liaison
Informational roles with examples: monitor, disseminator, spokesperson
Decisional roles with examples: entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator, negotiator
Efficiency (doing things right) vs effectiveness (doing the right things), linked to the manager's decisions
Mention level of management and the skills needed (Katz: conceptual at the top)

written.q: Explain why 'early management theory' developed when it did. Identify and explain two factors that created a need for more formal approaches to organising, supervising and controlling work.
points: Context: Industrial Revolution, rapid industrialisation, economic growth
Factor 1: large factories and mass standardised production needed coordination
Factor 2: large, often unskilled workforce needed supervision and training
Work before was rule-of-thumb and inconsistent, so it was inefficient with poor quality
Link each factor to the need to organise, supervise AND control

written.q: Analyse how organisations could benefit from early management theory. Apply your answer to two contrasting types of organisation, and explain which organisations would benefit from this approach, giving reasons.
points: Benefits: efficiency, consistency, standardisation, clear structure and lines of authority
Organisation 1 (benefits): e.g. Ryanair or a call centre needs standard, fast, repeatable processes
Organisation 2 (contrasting, doesn't benefit): e.g. Electric Picnic or a games studio needs creativity and flexibility
Name specific principles: Taylor's standardisation, Fayol's unity of command, scalar chain
Conclusion: suits stable, high-volume, routine work, not innovation-driven work

written.q: What was Taylor's contribution to management theory? Explain his principles and the problem each one solved.
points: Scientific study of tasks (time and motion) replaced rule-of-thumb
Standardisation fixed inconsistency, so quality improved
Scientific selection and training put the right worker on the right job
Piece-rate incentive pay increased output
Managers plan, workers execute: a clear division of responsibility
Legacy: efficiency thinking in modern operations (fast food, logistics)

written.q: Distinguish between Taylor's scientific management and Fayol's administrative theory. Explain four of Fayol's principles with examples.
points: Taylor: task level, the efficiency of individual work · Fayol: the whole organisation and top managers
TUS example: Taylor times registrations, Fayol designs departments and lines of command
Division of work: specialisation (bank tellers vs loan officers)
Unity of command: one boss (the 12% vs 6% discount conflict)
Scalar chain: a clear line of authority from top to bottom
Authority and responsibility: a foreman given a target needs the authority to draw materials

written.q: Explain Herzberg's two-factor theory and use it to advise a manager whose pay rise didn't improve staff motivation.
points: Two separate scales: satisfaction vs dissatisfaction
Hygiene factors (pay, conditions, policy, supervision) prevent dissatisfaction only
Motivators (achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) create motivation
A pay rise is hygiene: it removes complaints but doesn't create drive
Advice: job enrichment, more responsibility, recognition schemes, progression pathways

written.q: Outline the findings of Elton Mayo's Hawthorne Studies and their importance for managers today.
points: Western Electric, Chicago, 1924–33, the start of the behavioural school
Hawthorne effect: output rose because workers felt observed and valued
Informal groups exert strong social control over work habits
Recognition, belonging and security matter more than physical conditions, and money isn't the only motivator
Today: teamwork, employee engagement, supervisors' influence, wellbeing initiatives

written.q: Explain Maslow's hierarchy of needs and how a manager could use it to motivate staff.
points: Five levels, bottom up: physiological, safety, social, esteem, self-actualisation
Lower needs must be met first, and a satisfied need no longer motivates
Workplace example for each level (pay, contract security, team events, recognition, challenging projects)
Manager should identify where each employee is and target the next level
Limitation: people differ, and needs aren't always in strict order

written.q: Using PESTEL and SWOT, analyse the business environment of an Irish business of your choice.
points: PESTEL: at least one specific factor for each letter, applied to THAT business
Distinguish internal (S, W) from external (O, T)
Opportunities and threats drawn from the PESTEL findings
Link: use strengths to exploit opportunities, address weaknesses exposed to threats
A recommendation or conclusion for management
